Previous studies indicate that the routing of U.S. news through geographically determined sections can accelerate the spread of misinformation, yet the empirical evidence has been limited to small scales. Disruptions in electricity supply, whether caused by natural disasters, armed conflicts, or infrastructure failures, have profound consequences on essential services and economic stability. The results indicate that accounting for private vehicle behavior is essential for accurate network analysis and that the proposed optimization framework is well-suited for this purpose. Furthermore, integrating mobile charging with strategic movements of privately owned electric vehicles yields superior outcomes for mobile deployability and overall resilience, outperforming reliance solely on fixed infrastructure.

This paper introduces the concept of Input-Constrained Control Barrier Functions (ICCBF) to synthesize secure controllers for affine control systems operating within restricted state and input domains. A second contribution establishes a linking framework between ICCBFs and previously introduced Input-Limited Control Lyapunov Functions (ILCLs) from \cite{chen2020unified}, enabling the simultaneous satisfaction of all control limits during control transformation. We demonstrate that if an affine system admits an ICCBF under specific control restrictions, a supervising controller can be constructed to guarantee forward invariance of the safe set. We further analyze the robustness of this security controller against bounded disturbances. The proposed methodology is validated in a case study ensuring safe human robot interaction.

This paper introduces a new shared envelope formalism designed to unify the implementation of diverse, modern statistical packages. By offering this unified interface and runtime approach, the system promotes significant code reuse, resulting in streamlined distributions and "green" computing practices. Empirical results demonstrate that a single shared engine, built using this novel formalism, can successfully emulate ten leading statistical applications, replacing their distinct runtimes with a single, common infrastructure to achieve substantial efficiency.

This paper examines self-supervised scene generation for autonomous driving, a task where the goal is to master the visual complexities of traffic scenes sufficient to help driving assistance models reach human-level accuracy. Sundials were once a ubiquitous instrument for indicating the passage of time across human history, relying on the casting of artificial or natural shadows by the sun. Once thought obsolete due to the advent of more precise and all-encompassing atomic and digital clocks, these timepieces have garnered significant attention. We have gathered an collection of Indonesian sundials through our project, named **Suryakala-Nusantara**. Found primarily in open environments such as nature reserves, public squares, and park areas, these sundials vary widely in design, scale, and ornamental detail. Our study focuses on three main aspects: the temporal and geographical limitations of the shadows used to measure time, the classification system for the various types of sundials present in the collection, and the numerical methods used to translate shadow data into time readings. Our findings demonstrate that the shadows were calibrated for specific time and date conditions, and we established a comprehensive classification system for the sundials.

This paper introduces a novel integrated data transmission and wireless charging system relying on Intellect Reflecting Surfaces (IRS). In this configuration, a Data Transmission Device (D2D) pair exchanges information for a single user while concurrently charging another D2D user. The communication link is structured so that the data-transmitting source sends information directly to the first target, charges it using IRS assistance, and simultaneously delivers energy to the second charging user via IRS help. Consequently, this method avoids blocking nearby connections, thereby enhancing overall system performance. To support this framework, two optimization problems are formulated with the shared objective of maximizing the sum data rate: the initial problem focuses on jointly optimizing transmit beamformers, IRS passive matrix coefficients, and charging power allocation; the subsequent problem refines this by maximizing data rates through a big-step size (BS) algorithm, which simplifies the original objective by fixing IRS parameters. Numerical simulations confirm that this proposed approach outperforms both decoupled strategies and a baseline scenario where connections are separated.

Current approaches for matching summaries to articles heavily rely on the ROUGE metric, which assesses similarity by calculating the $n$-gram overlap between them. The proposed methodology trains a classifier to identify the generating source of a specific summary through a model with restricted capacity, specifically employing a character-level conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). By evaluating this enhancement via an article identification task using the matching dataset comprising press summaries against their respective newspaper sources, the authors report successful results. Full details, along with the provided codes for implementing this proposed method, are available at https://github.com/rahulshukla99/AI-NLP-SNLI.

Deep learning methods for visual–navigation (VO) and localization have seen significant success on image sensors due to their rich color and texture data, yet these modalities struggle with non-reflective or outdoor scenes. Conversely, 3D LiDAR sensors offer robust alternatives for indoor and outdoor applications, although they are limited by insufficient semantic or textural detail. This study proposes an attention-driven deep learning framework for 3D LiDAR-based localization that overcomes these semantic limitations. By integrating a set of pre-trained, state-of-the-art semantic image encoders as a semantic branch working in parallel with a standard 3D feature extraction network, the model fuses fused features from both domains to create comprehensive representations. Extensive benchmarks on two prominent indoor and outdoor localization datasets confirm that this proposed framework achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.

True mastery of Natural Language Understanding (NLU) requires the ability to grapple with linguistically difficult inputs, particularly sentences with negation that challenge logical reasoning. In standard federated learning, clients send their local model updates to the server during each training round for centralization. Yet, in practice, many updates are constrained by protocols like differential privacy, secure multiplicative inference, or bandwidth protocols, which alter the model parameters other than through minimal scaling or model averaging. We introduce a new federated modeling technique, termed Buffered Asynchronous Stochastic Deep Learning (BASDL), that trains neural networks even when model aggregations occur unconstrained by these modifications. In our method, a server maintains separate queues for each specific model version; private adjustments are applied directly during asynchronous batching and grouped according to the Bloom algorithm to prevent redundant calculations caused by private changes. Our experimental results using various neural architectures demonstrate that our model is faster than existing asynchronous strategies by up to 35% while utilizing identical computational resources per training cycle.

We examine the mechanics of fractures within solid rafts adhered to expanding substrates, whether through thermal expansion or other means. We also investigate how the probability of cracking responds to non-thermal external stresses applied to the environment. Our findings have direct applications to understanding physical phenomena such as desert road cracking and biological processes, specifically the growth-induced fractures seen in muscles and tendons.

We have created a three-dimensional numerical model for a multi-armed spiral galaxy resembling the Milky Way, featuring a four-armed spiral pattern. For each velocity scenario, we ran three distinct models: a pure hydrodynamic (HH) simulation, a code without full coupling between the fluids and magnetic components (M), and a fully coupled code (FC).

Observations from the simulations indicate that while galaxies merge regardless of the underlying physical model in all four speed cases, the presence and treatment of magnetic fields significantly alter the final configuration of the stars and gas. In speed regimes slower than 50 km/s—where both merging and significant gas restructuring occur—the predictions of the coupled code differ even more substantially from HH results. These discrepancies suggest that the evolution of the magnetic component is a crucial factor in cosmological merger studies.

Accurately forecasting the probability and size of market breaks is crucial for investors, financial institutions, and central banks to support their investment choices, risk management strategies, and monetary policies. Traditional models for tail risk, such as Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES), rely on heavy assumptions about normal market conditions, which often leads to underestimating actual market risk. More advanced models, such as GARCH variants, have been developed to better capture market volatility across various scenarios; yet, these typically produce risk estimates that are too rigid for the dynamic nature of actual markets. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework to achieve a flexible threshold-GARCH (TGARCH) approach that can more effectively forecast volatility thresholds under different market states through the introduction of an asymmetric threshold parameter. Within the proposed Bayesian structure, closed-form solutions are derived for the asymmetric threshold using a stepwise Bayesian procedure, which also specifies an optimal model selection strategy to choose the most suitable GARCH architecture. Back-tests on U.S. equity and currency data indicate that this Bayesian threshold-GARCH method outper both normal models and standard GARCH approaches in forecasting equity and foreign exchange volatility thresholds, with the resulting forecasts proving useful for optimal portfolio allocation.

Parameter estimation derived from pulsar timing data stands as a pivotal method for constraining fundamental physics-related general relativity parameters. Given that these timing parameters typically rely on maximum likelihood techniques, the associated likelihood landscapes are complex, irregular, and multimodal, further hindering reliable parameter inference. To navigate these challenges, this study applies a Bayesian approach utilizing the Nested Sampling framework to quantify the uncertainty and distribution of estimators. Additionally, because the computational cost of sample generation via this method is substantial, we investigate the advantages of a multi-core parallel processing strategy to substantially accelerate execution speeds. The proposed techniques are validated through a thorough analysis of both a synthetic dataset mimicking realistic systematic noise and actual observational data from the European Pulsar Array. These methods demonstrate the necessary methods to effectively characterize generalized noise models, thereby fully capturing stochastic variability in pulsar timing samples and accurately assessing the evidence for various hypotheses about fundamental physics generalities.

While their critical exponents dictate this universality, the most striking physical phenomena—phase transitions and symmetry breaking—arise because systems remain in the vicinity of fixed points for a finite range of parameters, guided by their flow toward critical surfaces. Our findings reveal precise critical thresholds and a close alignment with critical exponents derived from perturbative loops for both models. Curiosity serves as an essential catalyst for cognitive growth in both individuals and groups. While researchers have examined curiosity within single subjects or through neural imaging, investigating its manifestation in small-group settings remains an understudied area. This paper presents a novel approach to analyze the intricate, multimodal expression of curiosity in small-group environments. Specifically, it examines the drivers of sudden spikes in group-wide curiosity, termed "group surges." Utilizing a dataset of seven face-to-face problem-solving sessions involving pairs or small trios, we recorded high-frequency audio and video. After identifying surge events via natural language processing and behavioral metrics, we applied a causal discovery algorithm to extract the underlying causal structure linking surges to multimodal data. The resulting model identifies a dual-path mechanism for group-surged curiosity: individual-focused paths, where participants seek clarification on personal doubts, and social-oriented paths, where clarification is sought collaboratively within the group dynamic. These initial findings offer a robust foundation for further exploration into curiosity within social contexts, thereby aiding the development of enhanced group-based learning strategies.

Gaussian processes constitute a prominent method within nonparametric Bayesian inference for estimating functions with specific smoothness characteristics. These processes are defined by a mean function and follow the stationary assumption, implying their covariance relies exclusively on the distance between points—a property frequently modeled using Gaussian kernels, where smoothness is inversely connected to pointwise estimation variance. However, this stationary premise often fails when applied to irregular domains or graphs, especially where smoothness varies across different locations despite the lack of a regular grid for spline interpolation. To extend flexibility, this work introduces graph-based versions of Mat\'ern Gaussian functions that accommodate variable smoothness; although defined within general probabilistic frameworks, these models are implemented numerically via sparse precision matrix techniques, enabling efficient parameter inference and prediction with substantial computational savings.

In regions like nanophotonics and nano-electromagnetics, structures that are small on a scale of electromagnetic wavelengths but still significant on a computational scale often support highly accurate and efficient simulations using the finite element method (FEM). However, the time required for a standard FEM calculation typically scales with the cubic power of the linear resolution. This study introduces an accelerated alternative: a multipolar expansion scheme in which a fixed regular object is composed of a fixed arrangement of scattering and optical interaction domains. Crucially, while the number of coefficients per domain requires cubing to match the total computation count against FEM, the cost per domain can be reduced via scattering matrices or pre-computation, allowing the overall simulation time to scale with a low power (approximately 1.5) of the electromagnetic wavelength. We have applied this method, which achieves speedups of roughly 100 times compared to FEM, to our new algorithms for calculating multipolar expansions of electromagnetic scattering, optical force, and torque. These algorithms are versatile, functioning effectively for both transparent and opaque materials, and in cases of magnetoelectric coupling they often outperform specialized techniques that ignore such coupling.

Although artificial intelligence has achieved promising results in diagnosing diseases via medical photographs, the increasing specialization of neural models for single-pathologies utilizes standardized images that lack the natural variations found in real clinical environments. To address the gap between simplified examples and complex reality, this paper introduces an optimization framework for chest radiographs designed incrementally to incorporate patient-specific disease features into synthetic portraits. By leveraging this information during the visual generation process for tasks like medical image classification, our approach produces outputs that mimic both the physical characteristics of high-fidelity samples and the patient-level intricacies of actual medical radiography. Evaluating the associated image classification accuracy against state-of-the-art metrics using generated radiographs confirms a superior dual capability, achieving parity with the top-tier precision of existing methods while simultaneously mirroring the inherent patient-level accuracy of clinical data.
